claims.claim: AI dialogue drifts into philosophical debate rather than character-driven exchange.
claims.quote: AI dialogue more often turns into philosophical debate

claims.claim: Stories from five different LLMs cluster together in narrative-feature space while human stories are diverse; narrative features alone reach 93.2% macro-F1 detection.
claims.source: Russell et al., StoryScope; Dramatica gloss
claims.quote: five AI models cluster together in narrative space

claims.claim: 18% of professional writers' edits to LLM prose removed exposition that restated what was already implied.
claims.source: Chakrabarty, Laban, Wu, 'Can AI writing be salvaged?' (arXiv 2409.14509, LAMP corpus, 18 writers, 8,035 edits)

claims.claim: 17% of professional edits to LLM prose removed clichés and filler.
Awkward phrasing was the largest edit category (28%), e.g. the recurring hedge 'seem to (verb)'.
claims.quote: not technically wrong it's just inelegant

claims.feature: purple prose and lack of specificity
claims.claim: Professional writers' taxonomy of LLM idiosyncrasies also names purple prose (abstract words, excess adjectives/metaphors), lack of specific detail, poor sentence structure (20%), and tense inconsistency.
LLM literary prose produces metaphors that sound profound but carry no meaning the reader can cash out.
claims.source: Lincoln Michel, 'MFA vs. LLM', Counter Craft, 2025-03-17
claims.quote: Grief, as I've learned, is a delta

claims.claim: Within one passage the model jumbles construction, tailoring and magic metaphors without coherence.
claims.quote: protagonists cut from whole cloth, emotions dyed and draped

claims.claim: The AI story repeats its central idea with new metaphors instead of developing character, plot or thought.
claims.quote: doesn't really go anywhere. It's flat.

claims.claim: LLMs cannot make parts of a story work together because they have no point of view or intention behind choices.
claims.quote: They don't have a point of view

claims.claim: A 10,000-word story is ~10,000 choices; a 100-word prompt makes almost none of them, and the hardest work is shaping and refining.
AI sentences give the reader no place to stand because they do not originate from any sensibility.
claims.source: Charles Schifano, 'What's Missing from AI Writing', 2023-10-27
claims.quote: the sentences don't originate from anywhere

claims.claim: Sentences in AI prose can be reordered with nothing lost, because there is no point of view driving them forward.
claims.quote: there's no trajectory in these sentences

claims.claim: Asimov's editor, after hundreds of ChatGPT submissions: no originality, no narrative sense, no character development, near-nonexistent plotting.
claims.source: Sheila Williams, Asimov's editorial 'ChatGPT and Me', Jan/Feb 2024
claims.quote: no sense of narrative, no character development

claims.claim: Generated stories show no sign their maker ever absorbed a story, folktale or TV show; worse than any human submission.
claims.quote: ever read a story, heard some folklore

verdicts.trueWording: AI dialogue more often turns into philosophical debate.
verdicts.note: Dramatica blog (May 29, 2026) para on theme over-explanation carries the quoted sentence word for word. Caveat: the claim's contrast 'rather than character-driven exchange' is the analyst's gloss; the page does not use that phrase.

verdicts.trueWording: the five AI models cluster together in narrative space while human stories are more dispersed
verdicts.note: Quote is an exact substring. Both numeric halves confirmed on the same page: 'Narrative features alone achieve 93.2% macro-F1 in human-vs-AI detection' and the corpus of 10,272 prompts x five models (Claude, DeepSeek, Gemini, GPT, Kimi). Page attributes to Russell et al. StoryScope, April 2026 arXiv preprint.

Quote verbatim in section 4.4.2. Percentage confirmed: 'Unnecessary/Redundant Exposition (18%)'. Category defined as 'restating the obvious or providing details that add little value' and 'implied information' - matches the claim's 'restated what was already implied'.

verdicts.trueWording: Clichés (17%); 'unnecessary filler' is defined under Unnecessary/Redundant Exposition (18%)
verdicts.note: SPLIT SOURCING - the two halves come from different categories. 17% is confirmed for Clichés alone (defined as overused phrases losing original impact). The verbatim phrase 'unnecessary filler' is W2's gloss on 'fluff' inside section 4.4.2, the 18% exposition category already cited at index 152. So 'clichés and filler' at 17% conflates the 17% and 18% rows; recommend restating as clichés only.

verdicts.trueWording: This is not technically wrong it's just inelegant
verdicts.note: Quote verbatim from W1's email in section 4.4.6, which does cite "a very common phrasing in these excerpts is 'seem to _(verb)_'". Largest-category claim confirmed: 'the most common categories being Awkward Word Choice and Phrasing (28%), Poor Sentence Structure (20%)...'. Minor: the paper's category name is 'Awkward Word Choice and Phrasing', not 'awkward phrasing'.

verdicts.trueWording: abstract words, and excessive adjectives, adverbs, and metaphors
verdicts.note: No quote was supplied, so verbatim status is not assessable; every element checks out. Seven-category taxonomy (4.4.1-4.4.7) includes Purple Prose, Lack of Specificity and Detail, Poor Sentence Structure, Tense Inconsistency. Purple-prose definition matches the claim's gloss. 'Poor Sentence Structure (20%)' confirmed.

verdicts.trueWording: Grief, as I've learned, is a delta
verdicts.note: Exact capitalisation appears as a standalone pull-quote in the essay body. Michel's cash-out argument is on the page: 'Why is it good? If "delta" refers to the geographical delta then in what way is grief metaphorically a delta region...'. Note the line is the OpenAI story's text, quoted by Michel, not his own prose.

verdicts.trueWording: protagonists cut from whole cloth, emotions dyed and draped over sentences
verdicts.note: Quote verbatim. Michel's own diagnosis follows immediately: 'This is a case of what I've called the five-car metaphor pile-up... Nails and scaffolding conjure construction. Cutting cloth, dying, and draping are tailoring metaphors. Plus, you have a magic spell.' All three metaphor families in the claim are named on the page.

verdicts.trueWording: doesn't really go anywhere. It's flat.
verdicts.note: The two sentences are adjacent and exact ('...is that it doesn't really go anywhere. It's flat.'). Rest of claim confirmed in the same paragraph: 'The story lacks a traditional character arc or plot arc yet it also lacks an "idea arc"' and 'The central idea is just repeated with different flowery but incoherent metaphors.'

verdicts.trueWording: They don't have a point of view
verdicts.note: Quote verbatim; full sentence is 'They don't have a point of view or the ability to think about how parts work together to tell a story' - which carries both halves of the claim. Corroborated earlier: 'The author is a program that does not have a background, point of view, or artistic intention.'

verdicts.trueWording: The hardest and most time-consuming part of writing is shaping, honing, and refining
verdicts.note: Quote verbatim and is Michel's own sentence. PROVENANCE CAVEAT: the choices arithmetic is not Michel's - it is a block quotation from Ted Chiang's New Yorker piece 'Why A.I. Isn't Going to Make Art', reading 'a ten-thousand-word short story requires something on the order of ten thousand choices' and 'if you supply a hundred-word prompt, you have made on the order of a hundred choices'. Attribute the arithmetic to Chiang via Michel. Also, the page says a hundred choices, not 'almost none'.

verdicts.trueWording: the sentences don't originate from anywhere
verdicts.note: Quote verbatim. Full sentence supports both halves: 'There's no position for the reader to stand because the sentences don't originate from anywhere--you can't subsume yourself within the perspective of these sentences because they, remarkably, don't contain a perspective.' The claim's word 'sensibility' is a gloss on 'perspective'.

verdicts.trueWording: there's no trajectory in these sentences
verdicts.note: Quote verbatim. Reorderability claim confirmed in the same sentence run: 'You could, in fact, flip sentence number one with sentence number two and nothing would really change--there's no point of view, it is just a ceaseless, neutral, present tense, Nabokov replica.'

verdicts.trueWording: no sense of narrative, no character development
verdicts.note: Quote verbatim from the PDF: "There's no sense of narrative, no character development, and the 'plotting' is practically nonexistent." Preceded by 'There is absolutely no sign of originality or creativity in ChatGPT-generated works' and 'By now, I've seen hundreds, possibly thousands, of these "stories"' - so every element of the claim, including the 'hundreds of submissions' framing, is on the page.

verdicts.trueWording: ever read a story, heard some folklore
verdicts.note: Quote verbatim: 'There is no indication that the "writers" of these works ever read a story, heard some folklore, or watched a TV show.' The worse-than-human half is the next sentence: 'I have never read an original human-authored submission that was as poorly written or as uninteresting as these pieces are.' Minor: page says 'folklore', claim says 'folktale'.
